summaries.example: Imagine a red apple. Alyngton might ask: What is the apple itself? What size is it? What color is it? What is it related to, such as being next to another apple? He treated the apple as the main thing, while its size, color, and relations depended on it but were still real features.
summaries.summary: Robert Alyngton was a late-medieval philosopher and logician connected with the Oxford Realists. He was influenced by Walter Burley and John Wyclif, but he developed ideas of his own. He studied Aristotle’s categories, which are broad ways of sorting what exists. Alyngton said these categories first describe things outside the mind and only afterward describe the words and ideas used for them. He thought individual substances—such as particular people or animals—are the main supports for other things. Sizes, colors, and relations depend on substances, yet they are real features rather than mere inventions. Alyngton also defended universals: shared natures that exist in individuals and help explain why different individuals belong to the same kind. He tried to make language, thought, and the world fit together closely. For him, logic was not only about sentences; it also revealed how reality is organized.
key_ideas: Alyngton thought categories describe real things in the world, not just words.
He treated individual substances as the main things that exist on their own.
He believed universals, such as a shared human nature, are real outside the mind.
He studied how words and thoughts connect with the structure of reality.
He distinguished direct statements from statements that describe something indirectly through its parts or members.
summaries.why_it_matters: Alyngton shows that people in the Middle Ages asked deep questions about ordinary things: What is an object? Are groups and shared features real? How do words connect to the world? His answers help us see why debates about categories, properties, and general ideas have lasted so long. They also remind us that sorting and describing things can be a way of thinking about what reality is like.

important_terms.definition: A thing that exists outside someone's thoughts, rather than being only an idea or a word.
A broad kind or group, such as substance, quantity, quality, or relation, used to sort things.
A general nature that can belong to many individual things, such as humanity belonging to many people.
A particular thing, such as one person or one apple, rather than a kind shared by many.

questions_to_think_about: Is a color a thing by itself, or does it need an object to have it?
Can one idea, such as “animal,” really belong to many different creatures?
When we sort things into groups, are we discovering groups in the world or making them up?
Why might a philosopher think that studying language helps us understand reality?

summaries.example: Consider the statement “Humanity is running.” Alyngton would not treat humanity itself as a person who literally runs. He could allow the statement as remote inherence: running belongs indirectly to the form of humanity because at least one human individual is running. By contrast, “Socrates is white” is formal predication, because whiteness is directly present in the individual subject.
summaries.summary: Robert Alyngton, a late-fourteenth-century Oxford Realist, developed a strongly realist account of categories, universals, predication, substance, accidents, and relations. Influenced especially by Walter Burley and John Wyclif, he argues that the categorial scheme first divides beings existing outside the mind and only secondarily divides the concepts and terms that signify them. Being is analogous rather than univocal across the categories: substances, quantities, qualities, and relations possess being in different modes. His account of universals is also distinctive. Common natures exist actually in individuals, are really identical with them, and are formally distinct when considered as universal. This framework leads him to distinguish formal predication, where a form is directly present in a subject, from remote inherence, where a property is attributed through partial identity or through an individual instantiating a nature. Primary, individual substances are the fundamental substrates of existence; secondary substances and accidents depend on them while remaining objectively real. Alyngton also treats relations as forms present in both relata and explains second intentions as real determinations, thereby making logic an investigation of reality’s structural organization. His system modifies traditional Aristotelian categories by bringing logical and metaphysical analysis closely together.
key_ideas: Alyngton’s realism treats the ten categories as primarily divisions of mind-independent reality, with language and thought reflecting that structure.
Being is not a genus common to all categories in exactly the same way; it is analogous, since different kinds of beings possess it according to different modes and levels.
He accepts three kinds of universals: divine ideas, common natures in individuals, and mental signs of those natures. Formal universals exist actually outside the mind.
Primary substances are the ultimate substrates of existence. Secondary substances and accidents depend on them, although they remain real and are formally distinct from them.
His distinction between formal predication and remote inherence revises how essential and accidental predication are understood.
Alyngton gives relations an ontological status: they depend on a subject, an object, and a foundation, rather than being explained only by our thinking or language.
summaries.why_it_matters: Alyngton is important because he illustrates a late-medieval attempt to preserve realism while answering problems raised by nominalist critics. His work asks whether general terms correspond to real common natures, how properties depend on substances, and whether logical relations have an objective basis. The answers are not merely historical curiosities: they concern enduring questions about classification, meaning, universality, and the relationship between language and the world.

important_terms.definition: A broad class in Aristotle’s system, such as substance, quantity, quality, or relation; Alyngton treats categories primarily as divisions of extramental beings.

A general nature or item that can be instantiated in many individuals. Alyngton holds that formal universals exist outside the mind and are really identical with, yet formally distinct from, their individuals.
An individual, autonomous entity that serves as the underlying subject for other forms and properties; primary substances are substances in the strict sense.
A form or feature that exists in a substance, such as quantity, quality, or relation. It depends on substance but is, for Alyngton, objectively real.
A statement in which the predicate is directly present in the subject, unlike Alyngton’s indirect predication by essence.
Indirect attribution grounded in partial identity: a predicate applies to a subject through a shared constituent or through the individuals that instantiate it.
A feature of a common nature considered in relation to the many individuals that share it; it is not, by itself, the nature’s constitutive essence.
A relation that exists in both related substances at once, though it names only one side; its foundation is a quality or quantity connecting the relata.

questions_to_think_about: If a universal is really identical with its individuals but formally distinct from them, is that a coherent distinction?
Does treating categories as features of reality make logic more informative, or does it risk confusing words with things?
Why might Alyngton regard primary substances as more fundamental than qualities and relations?
Is “Humanity is running” a useful form of predication, or does its indirectness make the sentence misleading?
What is gained, and what is lost, by explaining relations through objective foundations instead of mental activity?

summaries.example: Suppose Maya and Leo are both playing soccer. The word “human” applies to each of them because Alyngton thinks they share a real common nature, not merely a label invented by people. But “running” applies directly to Maya or Leo, not to humanity as an abstract form. Alyngton could still say “humanity is running” indirectly if at least one human is running. This shows his difference between a direct statement and one that works through individuals.
summaries.summary: Robert Alyngton was a fourteenth-century philosopher, logician, and Oxford Realist. His major surviving work comments on Aristotle’s Categories, a system for sorting different kinds of beings. Alyngton was influenced by Walter Burley and John Wyclif, but he combined their ideas in an original way. He argued that categories first divide things existing outside the mind, and only afterward divide the concepts and terms that refer to them. He also held that being is analogous: a substance, a quality, and a relation do not possess being in precisely the same way. Alyngton defended universals, or shared natures. For example, humanity is a real nature present in individual humans, helping explain why they belong to one species. He described universals as really identical with individuals but formally distinct when considered in their different roles. Individual substances are the primary supports of existence, while accidents such as quantity, quality, and relation depend on them. His account of predication distinguishes a direct claim like “Socrates is white” from an indirect claim like “humanity is running.” He also gave relations and second intentions an objective status, showing his effort to explain logic through the structure of the external world.
key_ideas: Alyngton thought the categories describe the structure of reality before they describe words or ideas about reality.
He said being is analogous: different kinds of things have being in different ways, rather than all belonging to one single genus of being.
He defended realism about universals, claiming that common natures exist in individual things and explain why individuals can belong to the same kind.
Individual substances are the basic supports for other beings, including universal forms and accidental features.
Alyngton separated direct predication from indirect predication by essence, making his account more precise than an earlier version associated with Wyclif.
He treated relations and second intentions as grounded in the world, not merely in people's mental activities.
summaries.why_it_matters: Alyngton’s philosophy matters because it explores a question we still face: when we classify and describe things, are we discovering real patterns or only creating useful labels? His realism says that shared natures, properties, and relations have a basis outside our minds. Studying his view also shows how philosophers can borrow ideas from earlier thinkers while changing their meaning and building a new system.

important_terms.definition: One of the broad divisions used to organize beings, including substance, quantity, quality, and relation.
A shared nature that can be found in many individual things. Alyngton says such natures exist in the world, not only in our minds.
A particular thing that exists as an individual, such as one person or one animal.
A feature that exists in something else, such as its size, color, or relation to another thing.
A direct way of saying that a feature belongs to a subject, as in “Socrates is white.”
An indirect way of attributing a feature through a shared nature or through the individuals that have it.
A connection between things, such as similarity or being a parent and child. Alyngton treats relations as real features.

questions_to_think_about: If two people share a real human nature, how is that nature related to each person?
Why might Alyngton say that being belongs to different categories by analogy rather than in exactly the same sense?
Are qualities such as color and size real things, or only ways of describing substances?
What does the example “humanity is running” reveal about indirect predication?
Can language mirror reality closely, or does every classification partly depend on human choices?
